text:
Sampled HR@10 can conceal full-catalog ranking failures. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) show that sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; smaller candidate sets increasingly resemble AUC. The 2024 study [Evaluating Performance and Bias of Negative Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) finds that aggregate sequential-recommendation metrics hide head/mid/tail disparities and that negative-sampling choices change performance across popularity bands. Low sampled-pair loss therefore does not establish strong top-10 retrieval.

Practical diagnostic proposal: hold the trained NextItNet model fixed and score identical training-prefix targets against nested sets of 99, 499, and 999 unique negatives, plus full-catalog ranking where affordable. Compare uniform, popularity-weighted, and frequency-stratified candidates; report HR@10, target rank, and positive-versus-tenth-negative score margin, broken down by target frequency and history length. These are sensitivity checks, not calibrated estimates of full-catalog quality. [Time to Split (RecSys 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748164) supports successive temporal targets and shows that splitting choices can change model rankings. Targets already used to fit the checkpoint must be labeled in-sample probes; an honest rolling holdout requires training strictly before its cutoff.

For uncertainty, a practical extension is paired user-cluster bootstrap: reuse users, targets, and candidate draws across conditions, resample users within category, and recompute equal-weight category means and paired differences. Keep every prefix from a user together. Repeat candidate draws separately to expose sampling variability. Treat all diagnostics as exploratory; preserve the host splits, seeds, 99-negative validation evaluator, and macro HR@10 selection criterion.
